title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Introduction
content: The term “diphtheria“ is derived from the Greek word ‘diphtheria’, which means ‘hide or leather,’ owing to the characteristics of pseudomembrane produced by the organism itself over the site of colonization. [1] It is a vaccine-preventable but potentially lethal infection of the upper respiratory tract. The presentation may be as an asymptomatic carrier, cutaneous infection, or pharyngitis with the following manifestations, such as sore throat, fever, malaise, and cervical lymphadenopathy. The characteristic hallmark of the disease is the formation of the pseudomembrane on the site of colonization. Anterior tonsillar pillars and posterior pharyngeal walls are the most common sites of involvement. Before the introduction of universal vaccination in the 1940s - 1950s, it was the primary cause of disease and death in children and young adults. However, after the introduction of universal immunization, the incidence of the disease has been drastically reduced to approximately 5,000 cases annually worldwide. [2] Different factors, including low socioeconomic status, inadequate income, inaccessibility to public health, war and displacement, and ineffective monitoring of the immunization schedule, have led to frequent sporadic outbreaks of the disease around the world. In this topic, we aim to provide a refresher course on Corynebacterium diphtheriae .

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Etiology
content: Corynebacterium diphtheria is an aerobic or facultatively anaerobic, Gram-positive, non-motile, non-spore-forming, non-capsulated, toxin-producing, pleomorphic coccobacillus, which is usually club-shaped. Based on biochemical properties and colony morphology, it has four biotypes, namely, gravis , mitis , intermedius , and belfanti . C. mitis is responsible for mild, C. intermedius is an intermediate form, and C. gravis is a more severe form of the disease. [3] Substandard living conditions, low socioeconomic status, immunocompromised states, and incomplete immunization are risk factors for susceptibility and transmission of infection.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: The extensive implementation of a universal immunization program proved effective in reducing the incidence of diphtheria to approximately 70% by 1980. [1] Although there have been some occurrences of frequent outbreaks of disease in various parts of the world. The most notable outbreaks that occurred in the post-vaccination era were in several states of the former Soviet Union, with reports of more than 157000 cases and around 5000 deaths. [2] C. diphtheria outbreaks in Latvia during 2000-2009 reported the highest annual incidence rate in the European region, with a 10-year incidence rate of 23.8 cases per million person-years. [4] About 74% of the case-patients, including 93% of infants who died, were found to be unvaccinated. [4] This highlights the necessity for the universal immunization program.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: Nigeria reported its outbreak of respiratory diphtheria in 2011. A similar outbreak also occurred in India from 2010 to 2016. Diphtheria outbreaks were also said to have happened in Haiti, Venezuela, and Yemen from 2015 to 2018 as a result of inadequate income, poor access to health care, and ineffective vaccination and monitoring regimes. In 2017, outbreaks due to similar conditions were noted in multiple areas throughout the world, such as Rohingya refugee resettlement centers in Bangladesh and Indonesia. According to the WHO, 16,611 reported cases were recorded in 2018. [3] It is worth noting that these figures represent only the number of reported cases. Still, in general, the epidemiological burden of disease is far worse than what is seen on paper, mainly owing to a vast number of cases that remain under-reported, mostly in Asia, Africa, and Eastern Mediterranean countries.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: An active immunization schedule against the toxigenic strain of C. diphtheria may have effectively controlled the toxigenic strain. However, the non-toxigenic strain of C. diphtheriae is still prevalent and has now become an emerging burden of disease in developed countries. In the late 1990s, a severe invasive infection caused by nontoxigenic strains was reported in Europe, particularly in Italy, France, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Brazil. Among these countries, the most dramatic increase in the number of cases was seen in England and Wales, where the cases of non-toxigenic strain rose from 1 to 294 in the 2000s and have been increasing ever since.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is essentially a ubiquitous organism present universally in soil, plants, and animals, including humans. However, C. diphtheria is present almost exclusively in humans; although other animals, including cats, dogs, horses, and other domesticated animals, may also be potential carriers of this organism. [5]

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: The mode of transmission is via respiratory droplets or contact transmission from an infected host or their carrier. It can also be transmitted by direct contact with objects or secretions that have been in touch with the infected person or their carrier. After gaining access to the host, the bacteria usually colonize in the upper respiratory tract. They typically do not invade tissue to cause disseminated bacteremia.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Still, the toxigenic strains of these bacteria do produce toxins that are then released into the circulation, resulting in a wide range of clinical manifestations. Endosomes release Exotoxin, causing a localized inflammatory reaction followed by necrosis and tissue destruction. The toxin is made of two joined proteins. The B fragment binds to a receptor on the surface of susceptible host cells, which cleaves the membrane lipid layer, enabling segment A to enter. [6] Fragment A inhibits an amino acid transfer, thus inhibiting protein synthesis. Diphtheria toxin (DT) causes the catalytic transfer of NAD to diphthamide, which inactivates the elongation factor, resulting in a blockade of protein synthesis and, ultimately, cell death. [7] Local tissue destruction enables the toxin to be carried by blood and lymph to other parts of the body. Elaboration of the diphtheria toxin may affect the myocardium, kidneys, and nervous system.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Histopathology
content: Histological examination is not routinely carried out in cases with a high likelihood of diphtheria infection. Histology is primarily helpful for diagnosing Corynebacterium diphtheria , particularly when there is a co-infection with other pseudomembrane-forming bacteria, such as Staphylococcus species and Streptococcus species.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Histopathology
content: The initial stage of the disease is characterized by edema and hyperemia of the affected epithelial surface, followed by necrosis and the formation of fibrinous and suppurative exudates. These exudates then coagulate, creating a characteristic, sturdy, greyish-white colored pseudo-membrane appearance over the affected area. The pseudomembrane is composed of fibrin, necrotic epithelial cells, and C. diphtheriae bacteria. The membrane is composed mostly of fibrin over the vocal cords, while on the bronchus, it is composed of both fibrin and neutrophils. [8]

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Histopathology
content: The myocardium, if affected, may show extensive hyaline degeneration, accompanied by infiltration of mononuclear cells in the interstitium. There may also be areas of necrosis and inflammation present. Demonstration of diphtheria toxin (DT) within myocardial fibers can also be observed on fluorescent staining of tissue sections using an anti-DT antibody. On an electron microscope, changes within the myofibres, such as loss of matrix, mitochondrial enlargement with excess lipid, and disorganization of cristae, can be seen. Histological examination of the injured nerve reveals early changes in paranodal myelin, including both widening of the nodes of Ranvier and structural alterations in its configuration. Segmental demyelination is rare at this stage, but it becomes a characteristic lesion as the disease progresses. [8] Degeneration of axons is seen in severe cases. [3]

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Toxicokinetics
content: The production of toxins is the major virulence factor involved in the pathogenesis of the disease. The gene responsible for the synthesis of the toxin is encoded by a corynebacteriophage, which, when integrated into the bacterial genome, can potentially transform the non-toxigenic strain into a virulent toxigenic strain.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Toxicokinetics
content: It is composed of a single polypeptide chain comprising 535 amino acids. [3] Further analysis of the toxins via X-ray crystallography, along with genetic and biochemical analysis, reveals that it is composed of three functional domains, which are Catalytic domain with N-terminal ADP ribosyl transferase activity A transmembrane domain assists in the delivery of the catalytic domain across the cell membrane Cell receptor binding domain. After binding to the host cell receptor, the diphtheria exotoxin undergoes receptor-mediated endocytosis.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Toxicokinetics
content: The toxin is then endocytosed, where it is acidified within the endosome. The transmembrane domain is then inserted into the membrane, allowing the delivery of the catalytic domain to the cytosol. The catalytic domain catalyzes the NAD+-dependent ribosylation of elongation factor 2, thereby inhibiting protein synthesis. [9] Although the bacteria acquire a toxin-producing gene from a bacteriophage, its regulation is controlled by the bacteria themselves. The diphtheria toxin repressor gene (DtxR) is present on the bacterial chromosome, and toxin production depends upon the expression of tox and bacterial iron metabolism.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Toxicokinetics -- Regulation of Diphtheria Toxin Production
content: DtxR is a repressor gene that is activated by metals and is responsible for the regulation of iron uptake as well as the expression of haem-oxygenase and diphtheria toxin. [3] Siderophores are responsible for transporting the iron into the bacterial cell. Once the iron binds to the siderophores, a conformational change occurs in its structure, allowing the repressor to attach to the tox operator site. The regulation of tox by DtxR depends upon the availability of iron. DtxR is inhibited by a decreased iron concentration, resulting in increased toxin generation. [3]

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Clinical manifestations can be divided into local and systemic. Local signs occur at the site of colonization, where there is the production of greyish or whitish, black-colored necrotic membranes that ooze on removal. The most common location is usually in the tonsillar and the posterior pharyngeal wall. The extent of the layer can be correlated with morbidity and mortality, as extensive membrane formation can compromise the airway, leading to asphyxia and death. [10] Aspiration of this necrotic material can lead to aspiration pneumonia, which can further complicate the disease process. There is also a sore throat and cervical lymphadenopathy (due to enlargement of the draining lymph node, giving it an appearance of a bull’s neck). [5]

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Systemic manifestations can range from fever, malaise, shortness of breath, cough, cardiac and neurological complications resulting from circulating toxins released into the bloodstream. Cardiac manifestations can present as myocarditis, conduction defects leading to complete heart block, and severe heart failure. It can also lead to demyelination of nerves and the resulting neuropathy, ranging from mild weakness to complete paralysis. Some Guillain-Barré syndrome-like presentation has also been reported in the past. [5] It has also been known that diphtheria toxin (DT) can cause diphtheritic polyneuropathy via inhibiting the synthesis of myelin proteolipid and essential proteins, which presents as palatal palsy initially, then progresses to distal polyneuropathy, diaphragmatic paralysis, and eventually death. [3]

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Cutaneous manifestations can cause cutaneous diphtheria. It presents with an appearance similar to chronic nonhealing ulcers in exposed areas of the body, typically the hands, legs, and feet. It is clinically indistinguishable from an ulcer caused by other organisms and often coexists with Staphylococcus and Streptococcus infections.

[11] Hence, a proper mechanism needs to be in place to identify and effectively treat these conditions. [12] [13]

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: The diagnosis is clinical. Fever, sore throat, malaise, cervical lymphadenopathy, and particularly the presence of a grayish/whitish/blackish colored pseudomembrane on the tonsillar and posterior pharyngeal walls should prompt the provider to initiate early treatment with immediate administration of antitoxin. Diagnosis is confirmed by isolation of Corynebacterium species on culture and by toxigenicity testing. In equivocal cases, where the cultures are initially negative, such as due to recent antibiotic therapy, but with antibody titers being less than 0.1 IU in the serum sample and a known case of C. diphtheria in close contact, along with a positive PCR test of the patient, can support the diagnosis of Corynebacterium diphtheria . [3] Culture grown in Loffler’s medium appears as a metachromatic stain when stained with polychrome methylene blue (Albert stain). Meanwhile, a bluish-colored appearance is seen in the rest of the bacterial cell. [3] When grown on tellurite medium appear dark grey or black due to the reduction of tellurite to tellurium.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Evaluation -- Toxigenicity Tests
content: Elek Test: The Elek test is based on the principle of antigen-antibody precipitation. It was first described in 1949, and since its introduction, it has largely replaced the traditional in vivo virulence test in guinea pigs, which was most prevalent in those eras. In this process, a positive control, a toxigenic strain, and a non-toxigenic strain, or a negative control, along with a DAT-coated paper strip, are placed in the agar medium. After 24 to 48 hours at 37 degrees C, the presence of a clear line of precipitin at a junction where the toxins and the antibodies meet supports the diagnosis. Other enzyme-based tests, such as catalase, cystinase, pyrazinamidase, and urease, can be used to diagnose potentially toxigenic species within 4 hours. [3]

[3] Besides these, other tests such as ELISA and PCR have also been helpful.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Evaluation -- Imaging
content: Echocardiography can be used to assess the ejection fraction and identify other associated structural anomalies, such as aortic regurgitation, mitral valve regurgitation, and ventricular systolic dysfunction. Electrocardiography is an essential tool for monitoring dynamic changes in ST and T waves, which can detect conduction anomalies such as sinus tachycardia, ectopic beats, heart block, and myocardial infarction. CT scans can detect complications such as an interventricular abscess as well as changes in pericardial thickness. X-ray examination of a patient with diphtheria may reveal nonspecific findings, such as pulmonary infiltrates or cardiomegaly.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Evaluation -- Role Of Biomarkers
content: A rise in biomarkers, such as total leukocyte count and serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase levels (SGOT), can be associated with a worse prognosis and correlate with disease severity. [3] [10] Similarly, CPK, MB, and cardiac troponin can be used to predict disease activity.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Prompt administration of diphtheria antitoxin, along with antibiotic coverage, is the mainstay of treatment, as evidenced by some epidemiological surveys that claim it to be 97% effective. [9] Isolate all cases and use droplet precautions to limit the number of possible contacts. The diphtheria antitoxin or DAT is typically obtained from the horse’s serum, which has been immunized against diphtheria toxin. Hence, it is useful for neutralizing circulating diphtheria toxin and not for those toxins that are adhered to the cell. For this reason, it is empirical to administer antitoxin early after the presumptive diagnosis has been made, even before its bacterial confirmation.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: The antibiotics are administered to neutralize the offending pathogens. The most commonly used antibiotics are penicillin and erythromycin, which are usually given for a minimum of two weeks. It should be followed by nasopharyngeal and throat culture taken 24 hours after the completion of antibiotics. If cultures remain positive, a 10-day course of antibiotics can be added. There have been many concerns regarding the antibiotic resistance of bacteria. The first case of multi-drug-resistant C. diphtheriae, resistant to erythromycin, was reported by Mina et al. in Canada. [1]

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: A study conducted in Vietnam in 1998 found an increase in multidrug-resistant strains, with 4 out of 15 isolates tested resistant to erythromycin but still sensitive to penicillin. A similar portrait was also observed in Brazil, where seven out of forty-seven tested were found to be resistant to penicillin, while those resistant to erythromycin were two out of 47 [1], indicating that it is uncommon but possible for these organisms to develop resistance to a particular antibiotic.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Immunization against diphtheria begins early in life. Three initial doses are given at 4 to 8 weeks apart, starting with the first dose of the series, usually given in the second month of life. The fourth dose is given 1 year after the third dose, followed by a fourth dose approximately one year after the last primary vaccination. [9] Since the effectiveness of the vaccines gradually wanes over the years, the CDC recommends that the adult population receive a booster dose of the vaccine every ten years. [14] An additional treatment of diphtheria toxoid should be provided to a person traveling to an endemic area such as Asia, Africa, Central and South America, Russia, and Eastern Europe.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Corynebacterium diphtheria has many similarities with other disease conditions. The following are very close mimics of Crynobacterium diphtheria : Viral pharyngitis Streptococcal pharyngitis Acute epiglottitis Infectious mononucleosis Oral candidiasis Infective endocarditis Angioedema Epiglottitis Retropharyngeal abscess

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: The overall mortality rate of diphtheria has been relatively constant at 10% over the past 100 years. [15] The primary cause of death in patients with diphtheria is due to cardiac complications, where the incidence of developing cardiac complications following diphtheria is 10 to 30%. Still, of those affected, the associated mortality is approximately 50%. [15]

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: Several clinical and laboratory parameters determine an individual's prognosis. Clinical factors, such as an individual's immunization status, duration of symptoms, and time of diagnosis, influence the outcome of the disease. The extent of pseudomembrane formation [10] [3] and the extent of inflammation of soft tissue edema, which leads to the classical bull neck appearance, is associated with a poor prognosis. [4]

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: Laboratory parameters, including rising SGOT and total leukocyte count, are associated with poor outcomes. [10] A study conducted in 2004 to evaluate the clinical features and predictors of diphtheritic cardiomyopathy in 154 Vietnamese children found that the presence of extensive pseudomembrane and a bull neck appearance could more accurately predict the development of diphtheritic cardiomyopathy and, hence, the prognosis. [15] Similarly, the presence of myocarditis on admission, along with the presence of an extensive pseudo membrane, could best predict the fatal outcome. The elevation of AST was the best predictor for the development of diphtheritic cardiomyopathy.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Complications
content: Failure to timely identify and treat diphtheria leads to the dissemination of diphtheria toxin (DT) into circulation, which eventually gains access to the heart, CNS, kidneys, and other organs, leading to various complications. The cardiac complications can present as myocarditis, constrictive pericarditis, endocarditis, conduction defect leading to complete heart block, and, in severe cases, as heart failure. [16] [17] [18] [19] [20]

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Complications
content: Neurological complications occur due to demyelination of the nerve and the resulting neuropathy, which can range from mild weakness to complete paralysis. Some Guillain-Barré syndrome-like presentation has also been reported in the past. [5] It has also been known that DT can cause diphtheritic polyneuropathy via inhibiting the synthesis of myelin proteolipid and essential proteins, which presents as palatal palsy, initially progressing to distal polyneuropathy, diaphragmatic palsy, and eventual death. [3] The presence of bulbar palsy, the involvement of other organs such as the heart, and a less gradual onset of neuropathy of more than four weeks differentiate it from Guillain-Barré syndrome. [3] Other organ-specific complications include nephritis. [16]

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Socioeconomic factors, low-income status, unemployment, cultural and religious beliefs, false perceptions about vaccinations, educational status of mothers, premature birth, and parental absent-mindedness are some of the hindrances that affect the immunization status of an individual and, in turn, increase the likelihood of infection with a toxigenic strain of C. diphtheria . Certain health conditions, including dental caries, a heart condition, and diabetes mellitus, are associated with an increased risk of infection with a non-toxigenic strain of C. diphtheriae . Among these, intravenous drug or alcohol abuse and homelessness are major risk factors for contracting the disease. [21]

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Strengthening public health measures to ensure adequate immunization in toddlers, the adult population, and travelers to an endemic region is necessary to control disease outbreaks. An effective monitoring strategy should be in place to detect outbreaks in vulnerable populations. In addition, patient education through counseling, mass media, and other measures is essential to break the perception about vaccination and improve compliance.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Diphtheria is a potentially fatal infection with a fatality rate ranging from 5 to 17%. [3] Severe myocardial and neurological complications have been seen in two-thirds of patients with severe diphtheria. Myocarditis, constrictive pericarditis, endocarditis, atrioventricular block, and complete heart block are some of the cardiac complications. Most death in diphtheria occurs due to cardiac complications. Other documented complications include polyneuropathy and nephritis, which increase morbidity.

title: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The involvement of multiple subspecialties, including cardiologists, nephrologists, neurologists, infectious disease specialists, and surgeons, is necessary to improve the prognosis of the disease. Likewise, physiotherapists and rehabilitation therapists play a crucial role in the recovery of a patient with neurological complications. Ensuring adequate immunization status by a healthcare provider can serve as an effective prevention measure against contracting the disease in the first place, which can significantly reduce the burden of disease in a population. Nontoxigenic strains of C. diphtheria , though previously considered non-virulent, now emerge as an essential cause of endocarditis and pharyngitis. Hence, providers must diagnose and treat the condition as soon as possible.
